title: 3-Read Friday #115
author: Craig Barton
summary: This is EEDI's weekly curated '3-Read Friday' digest (#115), in which Craig Barton selects and frames three education blog posts. Article 1, James Tucker's 'In Defense of Doing Things Together,' argues that machine-driven learning is seductive precisely because it works, and that once efficiency rules, the shared, messy business of learning the same thing together starts to look like waste — quietly optimising away something schools exist to protect. Article 2, Chris Reid's 'The Idiot Who Talked About Discovery Learning at Interview,' complicates the tidy direct-instruction-versus-enquiry story, warning that the real risk is a quieter mutation Reid calls 'total instruction' in which teacher judgement is stripped out entirely. Article 3, Matthew Evans's 'The Use of Context in Assessment,' argues we fixate on the wrong thing with 'authentic' assessment and offers the borrowed idea of 'semantic gravity' — how a good answer moves between the concrete and the abstract — as a sharper lens.
points: The digest is Craig Barton's framed roundup of three blog posts he found interesting that week, each with editorial commentary.
James Tucker argues machine-driven learning is seductive because it works, and that efficiency-first thinking optimises away the communal meaning-making schooling exists to protect.

Chris Reid reframes the direct-instruction-vs-enquiry debate, warning the real danger is 'total instruction' — the stripping-out of teacher judgement — and that the evidence on method is genuinely mixed.
Matthew Evans argues 'authentic' assessment fixates on whether a task mirrors the real discipline, and offers 'semantic gravity' — movement between concrete and abstract — as a sharper lens.
Barton frames the throughline as a question about whether learning is inherently social, drawn from his AI in Education interview series.
quotes: Tucker argues that machine-driven learning is seductive precisely because it works — and that’s the danger. Once efficiency rules, the messy business of learning the same thing together starts to look like waste.
Reid argues that the real risk isn’t choosing direct instruction over enquiry — it’s a quieter mutation he calls “total instruction,” where teacher judgement gets stripped out entirely.
Having travelled my own road from well-meaning chaos to explicit instruction, I’m always drawn to writing brave enough to complicate the tidy version of that story
Evans argues that we fixate on the wrong thing with “authentic” assessment — whether a task mirrors the real discipline.
A borrowed idea, semantic gravity, offers a sharper lens: what counts is how a good answer moves between the concrete and the abstract.
